section_1a.directions: Section I, Part A — Multiple Choice: 55 questions, 55 minutes. Each question is followed by four answer choices. Select the choice that best answers the question or completes the statement. This part counts for 40 percent of the exam score. Work briskly; all questions count equally.

items.stem: The food cultivation system of the Native American groups referenced in the stimulus above is most analogous to which of the following North American indigenous food systems?

stimulus.text: Source 1: “He who is by nature not his own but another’s man, is by nature a slave; and he may be said to be another’s man who, being a human being, is also a possession.” Source: Aristotle, Politics, Book I (c. 350 BCE; Benjamin Jowett translation, 1885 — public domain). Source 2: Paraphrased from Mary Ann Glendon, “The Forgotten Crucible: The Latin American Influence on the Universal Human Rights Idea” (2003). Glendon argues that as Latin American nations gained independence in the nineteenth century, two intellectual strains merged with an older, more universalist natural-law tradition to produce a distinctively Latin American discourse of rights. She traces its roots to the Spanish Dominicans — above all Bartolomé de Las Casas, the sixteenth-century bishop who condemned slavery and defended Native peoples on the basis of a natural right to liberty grounded in a single common humanity: “All the peoples of the world are humans,” Las Casas wrote, “and all the races of humankind are one.” Following Paolo Carozza and Brian Tierney, Glendon credits Las Casas and his fellow Dominicans with laying the groundwork for a doctrine of natural rights independent of religious revelation, drawn instead from human rationality and free will and from Aristotelian philosophy.

options: Buffalo hunting among the Lakota Sioux
Wolf domestication by the Algonquians
Mixed agriculture among the Iroquois
Seal hunting among the Inuit

items.stem: All of the following features of the Constitution were designed to mitigate the problems described by Washington in the excerpt EXCEPT

stimulus.text: “…Let me now take a more comprehensive view, and warn you in the most solemn manner against the baneful effects of the spirit of party generally. “There is an opinion that parties in free countries are useful checks upon the administration of government, and serve to keep alive the spirit of liberty. This within certain limits is probably true; and in governments of a monarchical cast patriotism may look with indulgence, if not with favor, upon the spirit of party. But in those of the popular character, in governments purely elective, it is a spirit not to be encouraged. From their natural tendency it is certain there will always be enough of that spirit for every salutary purpose; and there being constant danger of excess, the effort ought to be by force of public opinion to mitigate and assuage it. A fire not to be quenched, it demands a uniform vigilance to prevent its bursting into a flame, lest, instead of warming, it should consume.” Source: President George Washington, Farewell Address, 1796

items.stem: The sentiments expressed by Jackson above would have been most shared with which of the following?

stimulus.text: “Is there no danger to our liberty and independence in a bank that in its nature has so little to bind it to our country? The president of the bank has told us that most of the State banks exist by its forbearance. Should its influence become concentrated, as it may under the operation of such an act as this, in the hands of a self-elected directory whose interests are identified with those of the foreign stockholders, will there not be cause to tremble for the purity of our elections in peace and for the independence of our country in war? items.stem: Which of the following best explains why South Carolina chose to secede from the Union in 1860?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Original diagram generated by the committed fixed-seed script gen_election_maps.py (this directory). No third-party source; electoral data cross-checked against published state-by-state results.
stimulus.text_stimulus: “On the 4th day of March next, this party will take possession of the Government. section_1b.directions: Section I, Part B — Short Answer: 3 questions, 40 minutes. Answer all three questions. Each question has three parts (A, B, C); write your answers in complete sentences. Question 1 is based on a secondary source, Question 2 on a primary source, and Question 3 on a non-text source (map, chart, image, or diagram). This part counts for 20 percent of the exam score.

questions.stimulus_text: Historians argue that few laws reshaped modern America as unexpectedly as the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965. Meant as a modest civil-rights correction to the discriminatory national-origins quotas of the 1920s, the act instead transformed the nation's demographics: by prioritizing family reunification and opening immigration beyond Europe, it brought millions of newcomers from Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. By 2000, nearly one in ten Americans was foreign-born, and cities from Los Angeles to New York were profoundly reshaped. The new immigration enriched American culture and the economy - but it also ignited fierce debates over assimilation, bilingualism, and the meaning of American identity.
questions.attribution: Original historian-style passage written for this item.
parts: A. Briefly describe ONE claim the passage makes about immigration after 1965.
B. Briefly explain how ONE specific law or policy changed immigration after 1965.
C. Briefly explain ONE political controversy caused by the immigration changes described in the passage.
exemplar: The passage argues that the 1965 Immigration Act transformed America more profoundly than its authors intended: by ending discriminatory quotas, it made the United States a far more diverse nation, especially through immigration from Asia and Latin America.
The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 abolished the national-origins quota system and prioritized family reunification, opening legal immigration to regions long excluded.

The new diversity sparked nativist backlash: critics argued immigrants strained social services and changed American culture, fueling debates over bilingual education, border enforcement, and - by the 2000s - comprehensive immigration reform.

questions.stimulus_text: They are well built, with good bodies and handsome features... They do not bear arms, and do not know them, for I showed them a sword, they took it by the edge and cut themselves out of ignorance. They would make fine servants.
questions.attribution: Christopher Columbus, journal entry, October 12, 1492 (abstract by Bartolome de las Casas).
parts: A. Briefly describe Columbus's impression of the Native peoples he met, as expressed in the excerpt.
B. Briefly explain ONE aspect of Taino culture that shaped this first encounter.
C. Briefly explain ONE consequence of Spanish colonization for the Taino within fifty years of this encounter.
exemplar: Columbus describes the Taino as physically impressive, generous, and technologically simple - people who had never seen steel weapons and did not understand their danger.
The Taino practiced gift-giving and communal sharing, which Columbus misread as childlike simplicity rather than a different cultural system of exchange and obligation.

Within decades the Taino population of Hispaniola collapsed - from disease, overwork in Spanish mines under the encomienda system, and violence - one of the first demographic catastrophes of the Columbian Exchange.

questions.stimulus_text: The following bar graph compares Union and Confederate military deaths during the Civil War, 1861–1865: approximately 360,000 Union dead and 260,000 Confederate dead, with disease listed as the largest single cause of death in both armies, ahead of battle wounds.
parts: A. Identify and briefly explain ONE conclusion supported by the data in the graph.
B. Briefly explain ONE way the scale of wartime death affected American society after 1865.
C. Briefly explain ONE limitation of the graph for evaluating Rhodes's argument about Northern and Southern attitudes.
exemplar: The war was extraordinarily lethal: over 600,000 soldiers died, and disease killed more men than combat, reflecting primitive medicine and unsanitary camps.
The enormous death toll produced national cemeteries, Memorial Day observances, and a generation of widows and orphans, while the South's heavier proportional losses fed Lost Cause memorial culture.
Casualty totals reveal the war's cost but not what soldiers or civilians believed; they cannot show whether the North and South misunderstood each other, which is Rhodes's actual claim.

section_2a.directions: Section II, Part A — Document-Based Question: 1 question, 60 minutes (including a 15-minute reading period). The question is based on 7 documents. In your response you must develop a historically defensible thesis, describe a broader historical context, use at least 4 documents to support your argument, use at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence beyond the documents, and for at least 2 documents explain how the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience is relevant to your argument. This part counts for 25 percent of the exam score.

dbq.prompt: To what extent did the Supreme Court advance or inhibit Progressive regulation of corporations in the period 1885–1920?

documents.text: "That the original design [of the Sherman Antitrust Act] to suppress trusts and monopolies … is clear; but it is equally clear that further and more comprehensive purpose came to be entertained. … Combinations are condemned, not only when they take the form of trusts, but in whatever form found, if they be in restraint of trade." —In re Debs (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: The Court upholds jailing Eugene Debs for the Pullman boycott; its purpose is to affirm federal power against labor, reading the Sherman Act broadly. Argument relevance: Use to show the Court's asymmetry: the Sherman Act was wielded against unions before it was used against trusts—inhibiting reform's allies while corporations went largely untouched.

documents.text: "Congress did not attempt … to make criminal the acts of persons in the acquisition and control of property … The contracts and acts of the defendants related exclusively to the acquisition of the Philadelphia refineries and the business of sugar refining in Pennsylvania, and bore no direct relation to commerce between states or with foreign countries." —U.S. v. E. C. Knight Co. (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: The Court voids the breakup of the Sugar Trust; its purpose is to confine the commerce power by separating 'manufacture' from 'commerce.' Argument relevance: Use as the leading case for 'inhibited': the Court gutted the Sherman Act against the era's great trusts, defining monopoly out of federal reach.

documents.text: "By the 14th Amendment … no state shall deprive any person of property without the due process of law … That corporations are persons within this amendment is now settled. [The Court] adjudged that the enforcement of the schedules of rates established by the [Nebraska law reducing railroad rates] … would deprive the railroad companies of the compensation they were legally entitled to receive." —Smyth v. Ames (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: The Court strikes down state railroad rate regulation; its purpose is to extend Fourteenth Amendment 'personhood' protections to corporations against state regulation. Argument relevance: Use to argue the Court shielded corporations from state-level Progressive regulation, forcing reformers toward the harder federal route.

documents.text: "The act [state law limiting maximum hours of bakers] is not … a health law, but is an illegal interference with the rights of individuals, both employers and employees, to make contracts regarding labor upon such terms as they may think best." —Lochner v. New York (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: The Court voids a state maximum-hours law; its purpose is to entrench 'liberty of contract' as a constitutional barrier to labor regulation. Argument relevance: Use as the signature 'inhibited' case: Lochner-era doctrine blocked Progressive labor laws for a generation.

documents.text: "The two sexes differ in structure of body, … in the amount of physical strength in the capacity for long-continued labor … This difference justifies a difference in legislation. … without questioning in any respect the decision in Lochner v. New York, we are of the opinion that [the Oregon law limiting women's working hours] … is [not] in conflict with the Federal Constitution…" —Muller v. Oregon (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: The Court upholds Oregon's women's-hours law on paternalist grounds; its purpose is to carve a narrow exception to Lochner without disturbing it. Argument relevance: Use to argue the Court 'advanced' regulation only selectively—protective legislation survived when framed around women's difference, not workers' rights generally.

documents.text: "The public policy has been to prohibit … contracts or acts entered into with the intent to wrong the public and which unreasonably restrict competitive conditions … The combination of the defendants in this case is an unreasonable and undue restraint of trade in petroleum … moving in interstate commerce, and falls within the prohibitions of the [Sherman Antitrust Act]." —Standard Oil Co. v. United States (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: The Court orders Standard Oil dissolved; its purpose is to show the Sherman Act could reach the great trusts—but only 'unreasonable' restraints. Argument relevance: Use to argue the Court 'advanced' regulation after 1900—yet the 'rule of reason' it invented also narrowed the Act, a double-edged precedent.

documents.text: "Viewed as an act establishing an eight-hour day as the standard of service by employees, the statute is clearly within the power of Congress under the commerce clause. Viewed as an act fixing wages, the statute merely illustrates the character of regulation essential, and hence permissible, for the protection of the public right." —Wilson v. New (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: The Court upholds the Adamson Act's eight-hour railroad day; its purpose is to affirm broad federal regulatory power over interstate carriers. Argument relevance: Use as the culminating 'advanced' case: by 1917 the Court sustained federal labor regulation under the commerce clause, marking how far doctrine had moved since E. C. Knight.
